## Learning from a sample

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

These are different weighting schemes, and they may target different quantities because their denominators represent different units.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An empirical proportion depends on which units receive equal weight. A token proportion weights every retained token equally. An average of speaker proportions first weights tokens within speaker and then weights speakers equally. These are different weighting schemes, and they may target different quantities because their denominators represent different units.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/index.qmd
:::

## Learning from a sample

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/03-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

It is: what can the observed speakers and clauses tell us about a specified quantity in a specified population?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Neither summary is automatically a population quantity. If the research question concerns speakers in a region, the population includes speakers who did not contribute to the corpus. The question for this module is thus not merely how to calculate a sample summary. It is: what can the observed speakers and clauses tell us about a specified quantity in a specified population?

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/index.qmd
:::

## Populations, samples, and estimators

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

An independent sampling model then states how repeated observations are related to a population parameter.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We begin by distinguishing populations from samples. The population must identify the units to which the claim applies, while the sample contains the units that were observed. An independent sampling model then states how repeated observations are related to a population parameter.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/index.qmd
:::

## Populations, samples, and estimators

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/05-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

An estimator is the rule that maps each possible sample to an estimate, while the estimate is the value obtained from the realized sample.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The pronoun case example uses a binomial model for one corpus proportion. Maximum likelihood selects the parameter value that assigns the greatest probability to the observed sample. An estimator is the rule that maps each possible sample to an estimate, while the estimate is the value obtained from the realized sample.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/index.qmd
:::

## Populations, samples, and estimators

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/06-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

Null hypotheses and test statistics compare an observed statistic with a reference distribution under a stated null hypothesis.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The sampling distribution of an estimator allows us to define its standard error, bias, and mean squared error. Confidence intervals and exact binomial intervals are procedures whose coverage is defined across repeated samples. Null hypotheses and test statistics compare an observed statistic with a reference distribution under a stated null hypothesis.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/index.qmd
:::

## Updating uncertainty with Bayes' rule

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/10-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

This order keeps the inferential target separate from the algorithm used to approximate it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The next distinction concerns prediction. A prior predictive distribution states what the model predicts before the present observations update it, while a posterior predictive distribution states what it predicts after that update. Both distributions put the prediction on an observable response scale. Other models leave a posterior that is mathematically defined but not available as a familiar normalized formula. We thus begin with a finite update, summarize it, derive a conjugate update, predict before and after conditioning, and only then turn to numerical approximation. This order keeps the inferential target separate from the algorithm used to approximate it.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/index.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/index/11-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0ba5430b9859dca9b2abb47c3a12a03ea353b7158fb74662802e88e1e138273e; role: concept -->

Markov chains and Markov chain Monte Carlo then permit dependent draws when direct independent sampling is unavailable.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The computational sequence also has an order. Monte Carlo integration first explains why averages of target draws approximate expectations. ## A finite linguistic population

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/populations-and-samples/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/populations-and-samples.qmd; note-sha256: c3fab91bc6880a85a7b75bb14fafa06d96eef8bce431ea7144a98081ebb589c9; role: concept -->

Native-speaker linguists manually annotated and cross-checked automatically preprocessed material.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We begin with UD Turkish BOUN, release 2.18, a Universal Dependencies treebank for Turkish, a Turkic language. Türk et al. (2022) describe the source and annotation process, while Marşan et al. (2022) document the agglutination-sensitive revisions. The release contains written sentences sampled within five selected Turkish National Corpus registers. Native-speaker linguists manually annotated and cross-checked automatically preprocessed material.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0
https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782

## Defining the objects {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/populations-and-samples/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/populations-and-samples.qmd; note-sha256: c3fab91bc6880a85a7b75bb14fafa06d96eef8bce431ea7144a98081ebb589c9; role: math -->

For a binary indicator $X_i$ that equals one when token $i$ bears `Case=Acc`, the finite-release proportion is

$$
p_{\mathcal R}
=\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal R}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal R}}X_i,
$$

where $\mathcal R$ denotes this release and $N_{\mathcal R}$ is its number of qualifying token rows.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## An observed sequence {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/independent-sampling/09-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/independent-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 6b559cb2a7cd4b35e6c779a359097ac601d2b0f6b6c95ede70a58ca0b2c73a04; role: math -->

The probability of this exact ordered sequence under the pooled working model is 1.082e-03. If the observed sequence contains $k$ accusative tokens, its product has the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathbf x\mid p)
&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}\\
&=p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The probability of this exact ordered sequence under the pooled working model is 1.082e-03. If the observed sequence contains $k$ accusative tokens, its product has the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathbf x\mid p)
&=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}\\
&=p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/independent-sampling.qmd
:::

A binomial probability for the unordered count would additionally multiply by ${n\choose k}$.

## From annotation to random variable {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/pronoun-case-example/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/pronoun-case-example.qmd; note-sha256: f9c1d362e1580411b97ec006968b414b5a86acbeccc6c5cde21dffc2c90bb34d; role: math -->

One row remains one personal-pronoun token nested in a sampled sentence. The binary response is a deterministic recoding of the source UD `Case` value:

$$
X_i=\mathbb I\{\text{case}_i=\text{Acc}\}.
$$

## From annotation to random variable {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/pronoun-case-example/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/pronoun-case-example.qmd; note-sha256: f9c1d362e1580411b97ec006968b414b5a86acbeccc6c5cde21dffc2c90bb34d; role: math -->

For $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, the two possible values give

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=0(1-p)+1(p)=p
$$

and, because $X^2=X$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[X]
&=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2\\
&=p-p^2\\
&=p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, the two possible values give

$$

=0(1-p)+1(p)=p
$$

and, because $X^2=X$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[X]
&=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2\\
&=p-p^2\\
&=p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\mathbb{E}[X]=p$ because $X^2=X$. Thus $\operatorname{Var}[X]=p-p^2=p(1-p)$.

## Probability and likelihood {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: ee3e3e51be423201bc5d8bdcd8f577668855d49c7de34f5fc7e3aebedea97c8c; role: math -->

For one observation,

$$
p(x_i\mid p)=p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For one observation,

$$
p(x_i\mid p)=p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd
:::

## Probability and likelihood {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: ee3e3e51be423201bc5d8bdcd8f577668855d49c7de34f5fc7e3aebedea97c8c; role: math -->

Conditional independence gives the probability of an ordered sample:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathbf x\mid p)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}\\
&=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k=\sum_i x_i$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conditional independence gives the probability of an ordered sample:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathbf x\mid p)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}\\
&=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k=\sum_i x_i$.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd
:::

## Probability and likelihood {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: ee3e3e51be423201bc5d8bdcd8f577668855d49c7de34f5fc7e3aebedea97c8c; role: math -->

As a probability distribution, this expression varies over possible data at fixed $p$. As a likelihood,

$$
L(p;\mathbf x)=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
$$

it compares parameter values for the data that were actually observed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

As a probability distribution, this expression varies over possible data at fixed $p$. As a likelihood,

$$
L(p;\mathbf x)=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
$$

it compares parameter values for the data that were actually observed.

[Sources]

:::

## Deriving the estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: ee3e3e51be423201bc5d8bdcd8f577668855d49c7de34f5fc7e3aebedea97c8c; role: math -->

The log likelihood is

$$
\ell(p)=k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The log likelihood is

$$
\ell(p)=k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd
:::

## Deriving the estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: ee3e3e51be423201bc5d8bdcd8f577668855d49c7de34f5fc7e3aebedea97c8c; role: math -->

Differentiate and set the score to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p}
&=\frac{k}{p}-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=0,\\
k(1-p)&=(n-k)p,\\
\widehat p_{\mathrm{MLE}}&=\frac{k}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Differentiate and set the score to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p}
&=\frac{k}{p}-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=0,\\
k(1-p)&=(n-k)p,\\
\widehat p_{\mathrm{MLE}}&=\frac{k}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd
:::

## Deriving the estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: ee3e3e51be423201bc5d8bdcd8f577668855d49c7de34f5fc7e3aebedea97c8c; role: math -->

The second derivative,

$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial p^2}
=-\frac{k}{p^2}-\frac{n-k}{(1-p)^2},
$$

is negative in the interior whenever both outcomes occur.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The second derivative,

$$

=-\frac{k}{p^2}-\frac{n-k}{(1-p)^2},
$$

## Constructing the sentence counts

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood/03-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: e921131fac12c2c8c69d656d64a6bfdbfb5b4d36a022853a8854433ebd42d5bb; role: concept -->

The zero rows lack recoverable document or register identifiers, so the analysis cannot model those sources of structure.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The full UD Turkish BOUN 2.18 release defines the sentence total used below. The pronoun extract identifies every sentence with at least one selected token; subtracting those distinct identifiers from the release total reconstructs the zero count exactly. The zero rows lack recoverable document or register identifiers, so the analysis cannot model those sources of structure.

## Deriving the Poisson estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: e921131fac12c2c8c69d656d64a6bfdbfb5b4d36a022853a8854433ebd42d5bb; role: math -->

Suppose, as a working model, that

$$
Y_i\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}}\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Suppose, as a working model, that

$$
Y_i\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}}\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda).
$$

[Sources]

:::

## Deriving the Poisson estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: e921131fac12c2c8c69d656d64a6bfdbfb5b4d36a022853a8854433ebd42d5bb; role: math -->

For one sentence,

$$
p(y_i\mid\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For one sentence,

$$
p(y_i\mid\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}.
$$

Course note: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd

## Deriving the Poisson estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: e921131fac12c2c8c69d656d64a6bfdbfb5b4d36a022853a8854433ebd42d5bb; role: math -->

The likelihood and log likelihood are

$$
L(\lambda;\mathbf y)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}
$$

and

$$
\ell(\lambda)
=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\right)\log\lambda
-n\lambda
-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(y_i!).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The likelihood and log likelihood are

$$
L(\lambda;\mathbf y)
=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda}}{y_i!}
$$

and

$$
\ell(\lambda)
=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\right)\log\lambda
-n\lambda
-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(y_i!).
$$

## Deriving the Poisson estimator {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: e921131fac12c2c8c69d656d64a6bfdbfb5b4d36a022853a8854433ebd42d5bb; role: math -->

Thus

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\lambda}
=\frac{\sum_i y_i}{\lambda}-n,
$$

and setting the score to zero gives

$$
\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i
=\overline y.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

$$

## Poisson maximum likelihood: answer 1

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood/12-answer; notes-page: statistical-inference/poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd; note-sha256: e921131fac12c2c8c69d656d64a6bfdbfb5b4d36a022853a8854433ebd42d5bb; role: answer -->

Zero-count sentences are part of the sentence population and contribute the factor $e^{-\lambda}$; excluding them would condition on observing at least one pronoun and inflate the fitted mean.

## Estimators are random variables {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd; note-sha256: adcb5696552e9e13ec3c4bfe34d452e43c04286e1fd9f8f3c7821c77b3025e96; role: math -->

For a sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the sample-mean estimator is

$$
T(\mathbf X)=\overline X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the sample-mean estimator is

$$
T(\mathbf X)=\overline X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.
$$

## Estimators are random variables {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd; note-sha256: adcb5696552e9e13ec3c4bfe34d452e43c04286e1fd9f8f3c7821c77b3025e96; role: math -->

Before sampling, $T(\mathbf X)$ is a random variable. After observing one sample $\mathbf x$, $T(\mathbf x)$ is an estimate. A useful sampling distribution is described by its expectation and variance:

$$
\mathbb{E}[T(\mathbf X)]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[T(\mathbf X)].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Before sampling, $T(\mathbf X)$ is a random variable. After observing one sample $\mathbf x$, $T(\mathbf x)$ is an estimate. A useful sampling distribution is described by its expectation and variance:

$$
\mathbb{E}[T(\mathbf X)]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[T(\mathbf X)].
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872
https://cran.r-project.org/package=phonTools
https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176344552
:::

## Standard errors

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/standard-errors/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd; note-sha256: 71fcc4683c7015e65e02c87fb4e27e60682dc92fb3cbe75222f415c091d7cb32; role: concept -->

The **standard error** of an estimator is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **standard error** of an estimator is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. We continue with the nonparametric bootstrap of the Hillenbrand cohort introduced on the preceding page.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd
:::

## Deriving the standard error of a mean {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/standard-errors/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd; note-sha256: 71fcc4683c7015e65e02c87fb4e27e60682dc92fb3cbe75222f415c091d7cb32; role: math -->

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent with common variance $\sigma^2$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[\overline X]
&=\operatorname{Var}[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i]\\
&=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}[X_i]\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent with common variance $\sigma^2$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[\overline X]
&=\operatorname{Var}[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i]\\
&=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}[X_i]\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd
:::

## Deriving the standard error of a mean {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/standard-errors/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd; note-sha256: 71fcc4683c7015e65e02c87fb4e27e60682dc92fb3cbe75222f415c091d7cb32; role: math -->

Thus

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\overline X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\overline X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd
:::

## Estimator bias {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/estimator-bias/02-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd; note-sha256: 418f47b66375ec5d46cfcc131a0bbc590c8e3d5597c20c425b5cb74365b2cca7; role: math -->

Sampling variability describes how estimates change. **Estimator bias** asks whether their sampling-distribution center coincides with a named target:

$$
\operatorname{Bias}(T;\theta)=\mathbb{E}[T(\mathbf X)]-\theta.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Sampling variability describes how estimates change. **Estimator bias** asks whether their sampling-distribution center coincides with a named target:

$$
\operatorname{Bias}(T;\theta)=\mathbb{E}[T(\mathbf X)]-\theta.
$$

## A target-specific comparison

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/estimator-bias/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd; note-sha256: 418f47b66375ec5d46cfcc131a0bbc590c8e3d5597c20c425b5cb74365b2cca7; role: concept -->

The median is not being judged as an estimator of the population median; it is deliberately being evaluated against the mean target.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We use the empirical mean adult-women /I/ duration in the Hillenbrand cohort as $\theta$. We compare the sample mean and sample median, both calculated from speaker-row resamples of the observed adult-women size. The median is not being judged as an estimator of the population median; it is deliberately being evaluated against the mean target.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd

## A target-specific comparison {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/estimator-bias/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd; note-sha256: 418f47b66375ec5d46cfcc131a0bbc590c8e3d5597c20c425b5cb74365b2cca7; role: math -->

For the mean estimator, linearity of expectation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\overline X]
&=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]\\
&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[X_i]\\
&=\theta.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the mean estimator, linearity of expectation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\overline X]
&=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]\\
&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[X_i]\\
&=\theta.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd
:::

## Mean squared error {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error/02-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd; note-sha256: cce745c11718644e54f9bdc00001391a366c52992d2f023a681f739a991b0fe0; role: math -->

Bias records systematic displacement from a target, while variance records sampling spread. **Mean squared error** (MSE) combines them:

$$
\operatorname{MSE}(T;\theta)=\mathbb{E}[(T-\theta)^2].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Bias records systematic displacement from a target, while variance records sampling spread. **Mean squared error** (MSE) combines them:

$$
\operatorname{MSE}(T;\theta)=\mathbb{E}[(T-\theta)^2].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd
:::

## The decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd; note-sha256: cce745c11718644e54f9bdc00001391a366c52992d2f023a681f739a991b0fe0; role: math -->

Add and subtract $\mathbb{E}[T]$ inside the square:

$$
T-\theta=(T-\mathbb{E}[T])+(\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Add and subtract $\mathbb{E}[T]$ inside the square:

$$
T-\theta=(T-\mathbb{E}[T])+(\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd
:::

## The decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd; note-sha256: cce745c11718644e54f9bdc00001391a366c52992d2f023a681f739a991b0fe0; role: math -->

Expanding and taking expectations gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{MSE}(T;\theta)
&=\mathbb{E}[(T-\mathbb{E}[T])^2]
+2\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]](\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta)
+(\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta)^2\\
&=\operatorname{Var}[T]+\operatorname{Bias}(T;\theta)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Expanding and taking expectations gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{MSE}(T;\theta)
&=\mathbb{E}[(T-\mathbb{E}[T])^2]
+2\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]](\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta)
+(\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta)^2\\
&=\operatorname{Var}[T]+\operatorname{Bias}(T;\theta)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd
:::

## The decomposition

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error/05-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd; note-sha256: cce745c11718644e54f9bdc00001391a366c52992d2f023a681f739a991b0fe0; role: concept -->

The cross-term vanishes because $\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]]=0$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The cross-term vanishes because $\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]]=0$.

## Confidence intervals

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/confidence-intervals/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd; note-sha256: d6ab656222d0983a8967073b76299fdb4505a41097d8e455d6d60c7f3a289c03; role: concept -->

Its coverage is a property of that repeated-sampling procedure, not a posterior probability assigned to one realized interval.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **confidence-interval procedure** maps each possible sample to a lower and upper endpoint. Its coverage is a property of that repeated-sampling procedure, not a posterior probability assigned to one realized interval.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd
:::

## Normal and t procedures {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/confidence-intervals/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd; note-sha256: d6ab656222d0983a8967073b76299fdb4505a41097d8e455d6d60c7f3a289c03; role: math -->

If $\overline X$ has standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$, a normal-reference interval is

$$
\overline X\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

When $\sigma$ is estimated by $s$, the one-sample t interval is

$$
\overline X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $\overline X$ has standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$, a normal-reference interval is

$$
\overline X\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
$$

When $\sigma$ is estimated by $s$, the one-sample t interval is

$$
\overline X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/confidence-intervals.qmd
:::

The confidence coefficient is defined through repeated sampling:

$$
\mathbb{P}_\theta\{L(\mathbf X)\leq\theta\leq U(\mathbf X)\}=1-\alpha.
$$

::: {.notes}

## Inverting binomial tail tests {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/exact-binomial-intervals/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/exact-binomial-intervals.qmd; note-sha256: 6d6cfa0710da747c5f825d8c659460aeb7b09501c8ad2518704ff3c02cb81800; role: math -->

Under $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$, the Clopper--Pearson interval finds parameter values whose binomial tails are not too small. For an interior count $x$, the endpoints satisfy

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_L}(X\geq x)=\frac{\alpha}{2}
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_U}(X\leq x)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Under $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$, the Clopper--Pearson interval finds parameter values whose binomial tails are not too small. For an interior count $x$, the endpoints satisfy

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_L}(X\geq x)=\frac{\alpha}{2}
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_U}(X\leq x)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/exact-binomial-intervals.qmd
:::

## Bootstrap confidence intervals

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd; note-sha256: 5d62af273e71350bd5ca04b6efd4a226578eade25a5fcee6a7553a3bc175061c; role: concept -->

The **nonparametric bootstrap** approximates it by repeatedly sampling observed units with replacement and recalculating the statistic.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The sampling distribution of a median is less convenient than that of a mean. The **nonparametric bootstrap** approximates it by repeatedly sampling observed units with replacement and recalculating the statistic.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd
:::

## The algorithm {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals/03-list; notes-page: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd; note-sha256: 5d62af273e71350bd5ca04b6efd4a226578eade25a5fcee6a7553a3bc175061c; role: list -->

For observed speaker values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$:

1. Draw $n$ speaker rows with replacement from the empirical distribution.
2. Calculate the bootstrap statistic $T_b^*$.
3. Repeat for $b=1,\ldots,B$.
4. Use the empirical quantiles $Q^*_{\alpha/2}$ and $Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}$ as percentile endpoints.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For observed speaker values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$: Draw $n$ speaker rows with replacement from the empirical distribution. Calculate the bootstrap statistic $T_b^*$. Repeat for $b=1,\ldots,B$. Use the empirical quantiles $Q^*_{\alpha/2}$ and $Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}$ as percentile endpoints.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd
:::

## The algorithm {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd; note-sha256: 5d62af273e71350bd5ca04b6efd4a226578eade25a5fcee6a7553a3bc175061c; role: math -->

Thus the percentile interval is

$$
[Q^*_{\alpha/2},Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus the percentile interval is

$$
[Q^*_{\alpha/2},Q^*_{1-\alpha/2}].
$$

Course note: statistical-inference/bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd

## One-sample t inference

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd; note-sha256: 285abdef335337ba687c921069293c3f8638f408e6b689c77a420bc1fce5e5c8; role: concept -->

One-sample t inference represents uncertainty in the mean of those speaker-level differences while estimating their scale from the same observations.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The paired Hillenbrand contrast yields one duration difference per adult woman. One-sample t inference represents uncertainty in the mean of those speaker-level differences while estimating their scale from the same observations.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd
:::

## From a standardized mean to a t reference {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd; note-sha256: 285abdef335337ba687c921069293c3f8638f408e6b689c77a420bc1fce5e5c8; role: math -->

For independent differences $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ from a normal population,

$$
\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{\sigma_D/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)
$$

and

$$
\frac{(n-1)S_D^2}{\sigma_D^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For independent differences $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ from a normal population,

$$
\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{\sigma_D/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)
$$

and

$$
\frac{(n-1)S_D^2}{\sigma_D^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd
:::

## From a standardized mean to a t reference {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd; note-sha256: 285abdef335337ba687c921069293c3f8638f408e6b689c77a420bc1fce5e5c8; role: math -->

Replacing $\sigma_D$ by $S_D$ gives

$$
T=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Replacing $\sigma_D$ by $S_D$ gives

$$
T=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd
:::

The corresponding interval is

$$
\overline D\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{S_D}{\sqrt n}.

## One-sample t inference: answer 1

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference/10-answer; notes-page: statistical-inference/one-sample-t-inference.qmd; note-sha256: 285abdef335337ba687c921069293c3f8638f408e6b689c77a420bc1fce5e5c8; role: answer -->

Replacing the unknown $\sigma_D$ with the random estimate $S_D$ adds scale uncertainty, yielding a $t$ rather than a normal reference distribution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Replacing the unknown $\sigma_D$ with the random estimate $S_D$ adds scale uncertainty, yielding a $t$ rather than a normal reference distribution.

## UCCA graphs across translation

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/paired-observations/05-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/paired-observations.qmd; note-sha256: 67ba45c349fa23a0c20817614fbdbce4916653c39c132a009b15442f27867194; role: concept -->

One row in the extract is one language side of a passage graph; the analysis unit is one of the 154 source-order English--French passage pairs.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

UCCA is a graph representation. A distinct **Scene** is a foundational node with an outgoing Process (`P`) or State (`S`) edge. A remote edge points to an already represented unit and does not create another Scene. One row in the extract is one language side of a passage graph; the analysis unit is one of the 154 source-order English--French passage pairs.

We apply the paper's paired estimand to v2; we do not claim to reproduce the paper's numbers.

The current v2 release is not the numerical release reported in the 2015 paper. The paper reports 583 sentences per language and mean Scene counts of 9.49 in English and 9.25 in French. The pinned v2 graphs form the aligned passage pairs loaded below and produce different graph-derived counts. We apply the paper's paired estimand to v2; we do not claim to reproduce the paper's numbers.

## Pairing changes the variance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/paired-observations/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/paired-observations.qmd; note-sha256: 67ba45c349fa23a0c20817614fbdbce4916653c39c132a009b15442f27867194; role: math -->

For pair $i$, define $D_i=Y_{i,\mathrm{fr}}-Y_{i,\mathrm{en}}$. Then

$$
\overline D=\overline Y_{\mathrm{fr}}-\overline Y_{\mathrm{en}}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[D]
=\operatorname{Var}[Y_{\mathrm{fr}}]
+\operatorname{Var}[Y_{\mathrm{en}}]
-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{\mathrm{fr}},Y_{\mathrm{en}}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For pair $i$, define $D_i=Y_{i,\mathrm{fr}}-Y_{i,\mathrm{en}}$. Then

and

=\operatorname{Var}[Y_{\mathrm{fr}}]
+\operatorname{Var}[Y_{\mathrm{en}}]
-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{\mathrm{fr}},Y_{\mathrm{en}}).
$$

## Paired means and alignment

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/paired-mean-inference/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/paired-mean-inference.qmd; note-sha256: e8ea056438d7b2d815af6441a6e59b1d16e3e08146a967c931341c829db33f2f; role: concept -->

The UCCA question is different: it concerns absolute agreement of graph-derived Scene counts, so the focal statistic is a mean absolute difference.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For ordinary paired-mean inference, one first forms within-pair differences and then performs one-sample inference on those values. The UCCA question is different: it concerns absolute agreement of graph-derived Scene counts, so the focal statistic is a mean absolute difference.

Course note: statistical-inference/paired-mean-inference.qmd

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/paired-mean-inference/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/paired-mean-inference.qmd; note-sha256: e8ea056438d7b2d815af6441a6e59b1d16e3e08146a967c931341c829db33f2f; role: math -->

For signed differences $D_i=Y_{i,A}-Y_{i,B}$, the target and estimator are

$$
\mu_D=\mathbb{E}[D]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\overline D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nD_i.
$$

## Comparing two independent means {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/independent-means/02-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/independent-means.qmd; note-sha256: 4a98d7bcb6f9462615ff8b3f11a94ec49e2c4fdbdd28f75ead6288004216f8bb; role: math -->

The estimand is the difference in group means,

$$
\Delta=\mu_{\mathrm{man}}-\mu_{\mathrm{woman}},
$$

estimated by

$$
\widehat\Delta=\overline Y_{\mathrm{man}}-\overline Y_{\mathrm{woman}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

When groups contain different sampled speakers, there is no within-speaker covariance to exploit. We compare /I/ duration in *hid* between the adult men and adult women in the Hillenbrand cohort. The estimand is the difference in group means,

$$
\Delta=\mu_{\mathrm{man}}-\mu_{\mathrm{woman}},
$$

estimated by

$$
\widehat\Delta=\overline Y_{\mathrm{man}}-\overline Y_{\mathrm{woman}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/independent-means.qmd
:::

## Welch's standard error {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/independent-means/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/independent-means.qmd; note-sha256: 4a98d7bcb6f9462615ff8b3f11a94ec49e2c4fdbdd28f75ead6288004216f8bb; role: math -->

For independent groups,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat\Delta]
=\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_{\mathrm{man}}]
+\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_{\mathrm{woman}}],
$$

so the estimated standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\Delta)
=\sqrt{\frac{s_m^2}{n_m}+\frac{s_w^2}{n_w}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For independent groups,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat\Delta]
=\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_{\mathrm{man}}]
+\operatorname{Var}[\overline Y_{\mathrm{woman}}],
$$

so the estimated standard error is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\Delta)
=\sqrt{\frac{s_m^2}{n_m}+\frac{s_w^2}{n_w}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/independent-means.qmd
:::

## Welch's standard error {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/independent-means/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/independent-means.qmd; note-sha256: 4a98d7bcb6f9462615ff8b3f11a94ec49e2c4fdbdd28f75ead6288004216f8bb; role: math -->

Welch's approximation uses

$$
\nu=
\frac{(s_m^2/n_m+s_w^2/n_w)^2}
{(s_m^2/n_m)^2/(n_m-1)+(s_w^2/n_w)^2/(n_w-1)}
$$

degrees of freedom.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Welch's approximation uses

$$
\nu=
\frac{(s_m^2/n_m+s_w^2/n_w)^2}
{(s_m^2/n_m)^2/(n_m-1)+(s_w^2/n_w)^2/(n_w-1)}
$$

degrees of freedom.

## Fisher's exact test

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/fishers-exact-test/03-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/fishers-exact-test.qmd; note-sha256: a79c9ebb2ab2e28a7202ed55d44e196fe798b41cb44e059e1602752c9572a1b5; role: concept -->

Its reference distribution is hypergeometric, so it is especially natural for a fixed sample drawn without replacement from a finite resource.

::: {.notes}

## The conditional probability {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/fishers-exact-test/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/fishers-exact-test.qmd; note-sha256: a79c9ebb2ab2e28a7202ed55d44e196fe798b41cb44e059e1602752c9572a1b5; role: math -->

With margins fixed, let $A$ be the front-vowel/*t*-initial count. Under conditional independence,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a)
=\frac{{K\choose a}{N-K\choose n-a}}{{N\choose n}},
$$

where $K$ is the *t*-initial column total, $N-K$ is the *d*-initial total, and $n$ is the front-vowel row total.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

With margins fixed, let $A$ be the front-vowel/*t*-initial count. Under conditional independence,.

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a)
=\frac{{K\choose a}{N-K\choose n-a}}{{N\choose n}},
$$

where $K$ is the *t*-initial column total, $N-K$ is the *d*-initial total, and $n$ is the front-vowel row total.

[Sources]

https://github.com/unimorph/tur
https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/
https://github.com/unimorph/tur/blob/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b/README.md
:::

## The conditional probability

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/fishers-exact-test/08-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/fishers-exact-test.qmd; note-sha256: a79c9ebb2ab2e28a7202ed55d44e196fe798b41cb44e059e1602752c9572a1b5; role: concept -->

R’s two-sided p value sums all fixed-margin tables whose null probability is no greater than the observed table’s probability; it is 0.5636.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The observed table has conditional probability 0.12016. R’s two-sided p value sums all fixed-margin tables whose null probability is no greater than the observed table’s probability; it is 0.5636.

[Sources]

## Expected counts under independence {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/chi-squared-test/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/chi-squared-test.qmd; note-sha256: bae11387d3da851107a292457a65273f04b03c594abd4f954641349024562852; role: math -->

For row $i$, column $j$, and grand total $N$, the fitted independence probability is

$$
\widehat p_{ij}
=\widehat p_{i+}\widehat p_{+j},
$$

so the expected count is

$$
E_{ij}
=N\widehat p_{ij}
=\frac{O_{i+}O_{+j}}{N}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For row $i$, column $j$, and grand total $N$, the fitted independence probability is

$$
\widehat p_{ij}
=\widehat p_{i+}\widehat p_{+j},
$$

so the expected count is

$$
E_{ij}
=N\widehat p_{ij}
=\frac{O_{i+}O_{+j}}{N}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/chi-squared-test.qmd
:::

## Expected counts under independence {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/chi-squared-test/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/chi-squared-test.qmd; note-sha256: bae11387d3da851107a292457a65273f04b03c594abd4f954641349024562852; role: math -->

Pearson's statistic aggregates standardized cell discrepancies:

$$
X^2
=\sum_i\sum_j\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

=\sum_i\sum_j\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}.
$$

For $r$ rows and $c$ columns, the reference distribution has

$$
\nu=(r-1)(c-1)
$$

degrees of freedom.

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/05-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: concept -->

## An exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: math -->

To introduce Bayesian updating, we posit an exchangeable superpopulation from which lexeme cells are independently drawn,

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta),
\qquad
\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

To introduce Bayesian updating, we posit an exchangeable superpopulation from which lexeme cells are independently drawn,

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta),
\qquad
\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1).
$$

[Sources]

https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b
https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/
https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/
:::

## An exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/07-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: concept -->

The committed 120-row sample was drawn without replacement from the known 588-row resource, so independent Bernoulli sampling does not describe that procedure.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model is counterfactual, not a description of the actual sampling design. The committed 120-row sample was drawn without replacement from the known 588-row resource, so independent Bernoulli sampling does not describe that procedure.

## Updating a continuous parameter {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: math -->

Bayes' rule for a continuous parameter is

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
=
\frac{
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)
}{
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Bayes' rule for a continuous parameter is

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
=
\frac{
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)
}{
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
}.
$$

[Sources]

https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b
https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/
https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/09-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: math -->

The denominator

$$
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
=
\int_0^1
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta
$$

normalizes the numerator.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The denominator

$$
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
=
\int_0^1
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta
$$

normalizes the numerator.

## Updating a continuous parameter {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/10-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: math -->

For $k$ focal cells among $n$ exchangeable Bernoulli observations, the likelihood kernel is

$$
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $k$ focal cells among $n$ exchangeable Bernoulli observations, the likelihood kernel is

$$
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
$$

[Sources]

https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b

## Updating a continuous parameter {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/11-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: math -->

Multiplying by the $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior gives

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
\propto
\theta^{1+k-1}(1-\theta)^{1+n-k-1},
$$

so the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior is

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(1+k,1+n-k).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Multiplying by the $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior gives

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
\propto
\theta^{1+k-1}(1-\theta)^{1+n-k-1},
$$

so the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior is

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(1+k,1+n-k).
$$

## What the posterior does not say

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions/16-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: a7d61efb0b0322bc3058c2b3d92799aa19f1621cd12afe293d556e99d1794055; role: concept -->

UniMorph supplies types, not token frequencies, so this posterior does not estimate the frequency of *t*-initial past endings in Turkish use.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The likelihood evaluates the fixed sample as a function of $\theta$; the posterior distributes model-based uncertainty over $\theta$ after conditioning on that sample. Neither quantity changes the known resource proportion. UniMorph supplies types, not token frequencies, so this posterior does not estimate the frequency of *t*-initial past endings in Turkish use.

## Center and spread {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries.qmd; note-sha256: 2861c6e73c0db287e2b818446095faf49770a1f36d74b1007be8c706bcdd29d8; role: math -->

For $\Theta\mid\mathbf z\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha',\beta')$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]
=\frac{\alpha'}{\alpha'+\beta'},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]
=
\frac{\alpha'\beta'}
{(\alpha'+\beta')^2(\alpha'+\beta'+1)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $\Theta\mid\mathbf z\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha',\beta')$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]
=\frac{\alpha'}{\alpha'+\beta'},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]
=
\frac{\alpha'\beta'}
{(\alpha'+\beta')^2(\alpha'+\beta'+1)}.
$$

## Center and spread

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries.qmd; note-sha256: 2861c6e73c0db287e2b818446095faf49770a1f36d74b1007be8c706bcdd29d8; role: concept -->

Neither center is automatically the preferred estimate without a loss function.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior mean is 0.352459, and its variance is 0.001856. The posterior median is 0.351650. The mean minimizes posterior expected squared-error loss; a median minimizes posterior expected absolute-error loss. Thus neither center is automatically the preferred estimate without a loss function.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries.qmd
:::

## Matching the summary to the claim

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries/14-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-summaries.qmd; note-sha256: 2861c6e73c0db287e2b818446095faf49770a1f36d74b1007be8c706bcdd29d8; role: concept -->

The row remains a lexeme--paradigm cell, and the independent-draw assumption remains a modeling assumption imposed for instruction.

::: {.notes}

A center answers a location question, an interval describes posterior concentration, and a directional probability answers a threshold question. ## Conjugate priors

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: concept -->

A prior is **conjugate** to a likelihood when the resulting posterior belongs to the same distribution family as the prior.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The posterior-distribution page normalized a continuous update by recognizing a beta density. A prior is **conjugate** to a likelihood when the resulting posterior belongs to the same distribution family as the prior.

## The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model likelihood and prior {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: math -->

The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model treats the Turkish UniMorph indicators as draws from a counterfactual exchangeable superpopulation:

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model treats the Turkish UniMorph indicators as draws from a counterfactual exchangeable superpopulation:

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta).
$$

[Sources]

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: concept -->

These are type-level rows, not corpus tokens, and the actual sample was drawn without replacement.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model likelihood and prior {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: math -->

For a $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ prior,

$$
f_\Theta(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1},
\qquad 0<\theta<1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ prior,

$$
f_\Theta(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1},
\qquad 0<\theta<1.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd
:::

## The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model likelihood and prior {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: math -->

Conditional independence gives the likelihood

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
&=
\prod_{i=1}^n
\theta^{z_i}(1-\theta)^{1-z_i}\\
&=
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conditional independence gives the likelihood

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
&=
\prod_{i=1}^n
\theta^{z_i}(1-\theta)^{1-z_i}\\
&=
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd
:::

## Collecting powers {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: math -->

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
&\propto
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}
\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}\\
&=
\theta^{\alpha+k-1}
(1-\theta)^{\beta+n-k-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
&\propto
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}
\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}\\
&=
\theta^{\alpha+k-1}
(1-\theta)^{\beta+n-k-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd
:::

## Collecting powers {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: math -->

This is the kernel of another beta density:

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This is the kernel of another beta density:

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd
:::

## Collecting powers

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/09-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: concept -->

With the support-calibrated $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior, the result is a beta distribution with shape parameters 43 and 79.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus the two posterior shape parameters are obtained by adding the focal and nonfocal counts to the corresponding prior shapes. With the support-calibrated $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior, the result is a beta distribution with shape parameters 43 and 79.

## What conjugacy buys, and what it does not

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors/14-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd; note-sha256: 483dac48daddc084e131e2f480d21d862dff9b52b9d96661768697eb7274d516; role: concept -->

The exchangeable Bernoulli model is a working superpopulation model rather than an analysis of uncertainty about the file.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The update is computationally convenient: it provides a normalized posterior, closed-form moments, and beta-binomial predictive masses. But convenience is separate from measurement and sampling. The known UniMorph resource contains 200 focal cells among 588, so the actual finite-population design is hypergeometric. The exchangeable Bernoulli model is a working superpopulation model rather than an analysis of uncertainty about the file.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd
:::

## From a parameter prior to possible counts {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 83a1ae94e3e31e471a22a9f2dee2027fc760f3d400eafb1603922aef305d3033; role: math -->

Under the counterfactual exchangeable-superpopulation design,

$$
\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
$$

and, conditional on $\Theta=\theta$, a block count satisfies

$$
\widetilde K\mid\Theta=\theta
\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\theta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## From a parameter prior to possible counts {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 83a1ae94e3e31e471a22a9f2dee2027fc760f3d400eafb1603922aef305d3033; role: math -->

The **prior predictive distribution** averages the binomial mass over the prior density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r)
&=
\int_0^1
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid\Theta=\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=
\binom mr
\frac{B(r+\alpha,m-r+\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **prior predictive distribution** averages the binomial mass over the prior density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r)
&=
\int_0^1
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid\Theta=\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=
\binom mr
\frac{B(r+\alpha,m-r+\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Nor does it describe Turkish usage, since UniMorph rows have no token-frequency interpretation.

::: {.notes}

The prior-predictive distribution belongs to the counterfactual independent-draw exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model. <!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 5ef5dd3889cd9a84f8c7baf77574edd5da8e9369265b83feea81333ec629f227; role: math -->

For one future binary value,

$$
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde Z=1\mid\mathbf z)
=
\int_0^1\theta
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\theta
=
\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For one future binary value,

$$

=

f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\theta
=

=

$$

## Predicting from the known remaining resource {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 5ef5dd3889cd9a84f8c7baf77574edd5da8e9369265b83feea81333ec629f227; role: math -->

The actual committed sample removed its rows from the pinned resource. If another block is drawn without replacement from the remaining $N_r$ cells, of which $K_r$ are focal, then

$$
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid N_r,K_r,m)
=
\frac{\binom{K_r}{r}\binom{N_r-K_r}{m-r}}{\binom{N_r}{m}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The actual committed sample removed its rows from the pinned resource. If another block is drawn without replacement from the remaining $N_r$ cells, of which $K_r$ are focal, then

$$
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid N_r,K_r,m)
=
\frac{\binom{K_r}{r}\binom{N_r-K_r}{m-r}}{\binom{N_r}{m}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd

## Two sources of posterior-predictive variation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions/10-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 5ef5dd3889cd9a84f8c7baf77574edd5da8e9369265b83feea81333ec629f227; role: math -->

The law of total variance gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\mathbf z]
=
\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z]
+
\operatorname{Var}[\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The law of total variance gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\mathbf z]
=
\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z]
+
\operatorname{Var}[\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd
:::

## A passage-level Student-t model

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: concept -->

Luke and Christianson (2018) describe the resource and its original measurements.

## A passage-level Student-t model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: math -->

We define

$$
y_j=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal N_j|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_j}d_{ji}
-
\frac{1}{|\mathcal V_j|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal V_j}d_{ji}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The course table contains one summary per passage, derived from 1,593 retained content-word positions. Each position was already aggregated across readers, so these rows are not participant trials. For passage $j$, let $\mathcal N_j$ and $\mathcal V_j$ be its retained noun and verb positions and let $d_{ji}$ be the position-level mean log first-fixation duration. We define

$$
y_j=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal N_j|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_j}d_{ji}
-
\frac{1}{|\mathcal V_j|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal V_j}d_{ji}.
$$

[Sources]

https://osf.io/sjefs/
https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/06-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: concept -->

It is not participant-level inference or a probability sample of English texts.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The resulting 55-observation analysis describes the unweighted distribution of passage summaries. It is not participant-level inference or a probability sample of English texts.

## A robust location--scale model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: math -->

The passage-level model uses

$$
Y_j\mid\mu,\sigma
\sim t_4(\mu,\sigma),
$$

with

$$
\mu\sim\mathcal N(0,(2s_y)^2),
\qquad
\sigma\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,2s_y),
$$

where $s_y$ is the observed standard deviation of the 55 contrasts.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The passage-level model uses

$$
Y_j\mid\mu,\sigma
\sim t_4(\mu,\sigma),
$$

with

$$
\mu\sim\mathcal N(0,(2s_y)^2),
\qquad
\sigma\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,2s_y),
$$

where $s_y$ is the observed standard deviation of the 55 contrasts.

[Sources]

https://osf.io/sjefs/
https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
:::

## A robust location--scale model

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/08-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: concept -->

The fixed four degrees of freedom make the observation model less sensitive to an extreme passage than a normal likelihood would be.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus both prior scales are computed as 0.103355. This is an empirically calibrated teaching prior, not a confirmatory analysis. The fixed four degrees of freedom make the observation model less sensitive to an extreme passage than a normal likelihood would be.

[Sources]

https://osf.io/sjefs/
https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
:::

## A robust location--scale model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/09-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: math -->

Let $\eta=(\mu,\log\sigma)$. The unnormalized log posterior on this unconstrained scale is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\widetilde f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\sum_{j=1}^{N}
\left[
\log t_4\!\left(\frac{y_j-\mu}{\sigma}\right)
-\log\sigma
\right]\\
&+\log\phi(\mu;0,2s_y)
+\log 2+\log\phi(\sigma;0,2s_y)
+\log\sigma.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\eta=(\mu,\log\sigma)$. The unnormalized log posterior on this unconstrained scale is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\widetilde f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)
={}&\sum_{j=1}^{N}
\left[
\log t_4\!\left(\frac{y_j-\mu}{\sigma}\right)
-\log\sigma
\right]\\
&+\log\phi(\mu;0,2s_y)
+\log 2+\log\phi(\sigma;0,2s_y)
+\log\sigma.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

https://osf.io/sjefs/
https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
:::

The Stan program later samples $\sigma$ directly and lets Stan handle its internal transform, so it does not add this term manually.

::: {.notes}

The final term is the Jacobian for $\sigma=\exp(\eta_2)$. The Stan program later samples $\sigma$ directly and lets Stan handle its internal transform, so it does not add this term manually.

## The missing normalizer {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/13-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: math -->

The normalized posterior is

$$
f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)}{Z},
\qquad
Z=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta'.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The normalized posterior is

$$
f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)}{Z},
\qquad
Z=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta'.
$$

## The missing normalizer {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy/14-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd; note-sha256: 450d22b6c1f186ae6434d2acc712134d9d5d202030b2accf81caa3aff347460e; role: math -->

The grid approximates $Z$ numerically, but later algorithms need only relative density or its gradient. For two parameter values,

$$
\frac{f(\eta_b\mid\mathbf y)}{f(\eta_a\mid\mathbf y)}
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta_b\mid\mathbf y)}{\widetilde f(\eta_a\mid\mathbf y)},
$$

because $Z$ cancels.

## Monte Carlo integration

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: concept -->

Monte Carlo integration replaces an expectation under that posterior with an average over draws while keeping posterior uncertainty distinct from numerical error.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The passage-level Student-$t$ model has no convenient closed-form posterior. Monte Carlo integration replaces an expectation under that posterior with an average over draws while keeping posterior uncertainty distinct from numerical error.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd
:::

## Expectations as integrals {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: math -->

For a target density $f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)$ and an integrable function $g$,

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\eta)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\eta)f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a target density $f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)$ and an integrable function $g$,

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\eta)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\eta)f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd
:::

## Expectations as integrals {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: math -->

Independent target draws give the estimator

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\eta^{(s)}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Independent target draws give the estimator

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\eta^{(s)}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd
:::

## Expectations as integrals

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/05-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: concept -->

Setting $g(\eta)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$ estimates its directional probability, while $g(\eta)=\exp(\mu)$ gives a central geometric-scale noun-to-verb ratio.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Setting $g(\eta)=\mu$ estimates the posterior mean of the passage location. Setting $g(\eta)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$ estimates its directional probability, while $g(\eta)=\exp(\mu)$ gives a central geometric-scale noun-to-verb ratio.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd
:::

## Drawing from the posterior grid

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/06-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: concept -->

The calculation reconstructs the passage-level Student-t model from the 55 passage summaries, normalizes its $321\times321$ reference grid, and samples 20,000 grid cells with their posterior weights.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

the calculation reconstructs the passage-level Student-t model from the 55 passage summaries, normalizes its $321\times321$ reference grid, and samples 20,000 grid cells with their posterior weights.

## Drawing from the posterior grid {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: math -->

The grid benchmark and Monte Carlo estimates agree to the scale of their Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs). For independent draws,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\widehat I_S)
=
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(g(\eta))}{S}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## Two uncertainties

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration/12-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd; note-sha256: ceeeb3714447006bf83cf12a982f9845d23c0cf17c8ad169c1c68a0d8a553296; role: concept -->

More draws are not more linguistic evidence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Posterior spread describes model-based uncertainty about the passage-level Student-t model. Monte Carlo error describes finite numerical approximation. Increasing $S$ reduces the latter but adds no passages, positions, or readers. More draws are not more linguistic evidence.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd
:::

## Importance sampling

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/importance-sampling/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 1db62839a56c79f528dbc4e9c523e746a8be9e4aca90c206b8098d43d04dfffc; role: concept -->

**Importance sampling** instead draws from a proposal distribution and corrects its mismatch with the unnormalized passage-level Student-t posterior through weights.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Monte Carlo integration used draws from the normalized posterior grid. **Importance sampling** instead draws from a proposal distribution and corrects its mismatch with the unnormalized passage-level Student-t posterior through weights.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd
:::

## Reweighting a proposal {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/importance-sampling/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 1db62839a56c79f528dbc4e9c523e746a8be9e4aca90c206b8098d43d04dfffc; role: math -->

For target density $f$, proposal density $g$, and integrand $h$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_f[h(\eta)]
&=
\int h(\eta)\frac{f(\eta)}{g(\eta)}g(\eta)\,\mathrm d\eta\\
&=
\mathbb{E}_g[h(\eta)w(\eta)],
\end{aligned}
$$

where $w(\eta)=f(\eta)/g(\eta)$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For target density $f$, proposal density $g$, and integrand $h$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_f[h(\eta)]
&=
\int h(\eta)\frac{f(\eta)}{g(\eta)}g(\eta)\,\mathrm d\eta\\
&=
\mathbb{E}_g[h(\eta)w(\eta)],
\end{aligned}
$$

where $w(\eta)=f(\eta)/g(\eta)$.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd
:::

## Reweighting a proposal {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/importance-sampling/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 1db62839a56c79f528dbc4e9c523e746a8be9e4aca90c206b8098d43d04dfffc; role: math -->

If the target is known only as $\widetilde f(\eta)=Zf(\eta)$, normalized weights

$$
\widetilde w^{(s)}
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)})/g(\eta^{(s)})}
{\sum_{r=1}^S\widetilde f(\eta^{(r)})/g(\eta^{(r)})}
$$

remove the shared unknown constant.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If the target is known only as $\widetilde f(\eta)=Zf(\eta)$, normalized weights

$$
\widetilde w^{(s)}
=
\frac{\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)})/g(\eta^{(s)})}
{\sum_{r=1}^S\widetilde f(\eta^{(r)})/g(\eta^{(r)})}
$$

remove the shared unknown constant.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd
:::

## Reweighting a proposal {.equation-slide}

The self-normalized estimator is

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\sum_{s=1}^S\widetilde w^{(s)}h(\eta^{(s)}).
$$

the calculation reconstructs the same posterior grid used on the preceding page. It then draws 30,000 values from a bivariate $t_5$ proposal centered at the grid mean with scale $1.5\widehat\Sigma$. ## Assessing importance weights {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/importance-sampling/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 1db62839a56c79f528dbc4e9c523e746a8be9e4aca90c206b8098d43d04dfffc; role: math -->

The raw-weight effective sample size,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}_w
=
\frac{1}{\sum_{s=1}^S(\widetilde w^{(s)})^2},
$$

is 23,991 from 30,000 proposal draws.

## Assessing importance weights

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/importance-sampling/11-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 1db62839a56c79f528dbc4e9c523e746a8be9e4aca90c206b8098d43d04dfffc; role: concept -->

The largest weight and the mass in the largest 100 weights diagnose that realized concentration but cannot prove that an unseen tail was covered.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The proposal must cover every target region of positive probability. Shared support is not sufficient for efficiency: if $q$ places little mass in an important target region, a few weights dominate. The largest weight and the mass in the largest 100 weights diagnose that realized concentration but cannot prove that an unseen tail was covered.

[Sources]

## Assessing importance weights

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/importance-sampling/12-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 1db62839a56c79f528dbc4e9c523e746a8be9e4aca90c206b8098d43d04dfffc; role: concept -->

Only the weighted empirical distribution approximates the passage-level Student-t model.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The proposal distribution is a computational device. Its unweighted draw frequency is neither a prior nor a statement about passage contrasts. Only the weighted empirical distribution approximates the passage-level Student-t model.

## Markov chains

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chains/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd; note-sha256: f9aa33aae87be9c4bdf55716833843a981e33f419c3f3c97b8cb9f44084c389a; role: concept -->

This dependence defines a **Markov chain**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The passage-level Student-t model cannot be sampled directly in closed form. We now construct a sequence of parameter states in which the next state depends on the current state. This dependence defines a **Markov chain**.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd
:::

## The Markov property {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chains/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd; note-sha256: f9aa33aae87be9c4bdf55716833843a981e33f419c3f3c97b8cb9f44084c389a; role: math -->

Let $\eta_s=(\mu_s,\log\sigma_s)$ denote the state at iteration $s$. For every measurable set $A$, the Markov property is

$$
\mathbb{P}(\eta_{s+1}\in A\mid
\eta_s=\eta_s,\ldots,\eta_1=\eta_1)
=
\mathbb{P}(\eta_{s+1}\in A\mid\eta_s=\eta_s).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\eta_s=(\mu_s,\log\sigma_s)$ denote the state at iteration $s$. For every measurable set $A$, the Markov property is

$$
\mathbb{P}(\eta_{s+1}\in A\mid
\eta_s=\eta_s,\ldots,\eta_1=\eta_1)
=
\mathbb{P}(\eta_{s+1}\in A\mid\eta_s=\eta_s).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd
:::

## The Markov property

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chains/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd; note-sha256: f9aa33aae87be9c4bdf55716833843a981e33f419c3f3c97b8cb9f44084c389a; role: concept -->

This does not make adjacent states independent: the proposal is centered on the current state, and rejection repeats it.

::: {.notes}

Once the current passage-level Student-t model state is known, earlier states do not alter the next transition distribution. This does not make adjacent states independent: the proposal is centered on the current state, and rejection repeats it.
