## Transition and stationary distributions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chains/07-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd; note-sha256: f9aa33aae87be9c4bdf55716833843a981e33f419c3f3c97b8cb9f44084c389a; role: math -->

Write the transition kernel as

$$
K(\eta,A)
=
\mathbb{P}(\eta_{s+1}\in A\mid\eta_s=\eta).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Write the transition kernel as

$$
K(\eta,A)
=
\mathbb{P}(\eta_{s+1}\in A\mid\eta_s=\eta).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd
:::

## Transition and stationary distributions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chains/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd; note-sha256: f9aa33aae87be9c4bdf55716833843a981e33f419c3f3c97b8cb9f44084c389a; role: math -->

A density $\pi$ is stationary when

$$
\int K(\eta,A)\pi(\eta)\,\mathrm d\eta
=
\int_A\pi(\eta')\,\mathrm d\eta'.
$$

That is, if the current state has distribution $\pi$, one transition leaves its distribution unchanged.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A density $\pi$ is stationary when

$$
\int K(\eta,A)\pi(\eta)\,\mathrm d\eta
=
\int_A\pi(\eta')\,\mathrm d\eta'.
$$

That is, if the current state has distribution $\pi$, one transition leaves its distribution unchanged.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chains.qmd
:::

Continuous-state conditions are more technical, and a finite run still requires diagnostics.

## Markov chain Monte Carlo

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: f4df3d0bb3f361ef3ff22052003fbcbaadb7f1a22f2777f87c30ad9355622192; role: concept -->

**Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)** uses dependent states from a chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior target.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Monte Carlo integration used independent draws from the passage-level Student-t posterior. Direct posterior draws are often unavailable. **Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)** uses dependent states from a chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior target.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd
:::

## Chain averages {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: f4df3d0bb3f361ef3ff22052003fbcbaadb7f1a22f2777f87c30ad9355622192; role: math -->

For the passage-level Student-t model and a function $g$, the target is

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\eta)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\eta)f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the passage-level Student-t model and a function $g$, the target is

$$
I
=
\mathbb{E}[g(\eta)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\eta)f(\eta\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\eta.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd
:::

## Chain averages {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: f4df3d0bb3f361ef3ff22052003fbcbaadb7f1a22f2777f87c30ad9355622192; role: math -->

Under conditions that make the chain ergodic,

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\eta^{(s)})
$$

converges to $I$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Under conditions that make the chain ergodic,

$$
\widehat I_S
=
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^Sg(\eta^{(s)})
$$

converges to $I$.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd
:::

## Three distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo/09-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: f4df3d0bb3f361ef3ff22052003fbcbaadb7f1a22f2777f87c30ad9355622192; role: concept -->

Conflating these three objects makes it impossible to say whether a problem belongs to the model or the computation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The posterior target is defined by the likelihood and prior. The transition distribution moves from one state to the next while preserving that target. The empirical distribution of a finite run approximates the target and contains Monte Carlo error. Conflating these three objects makes it impossible to say whether a problem belongs to the model or the computation.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd
:::

## Three distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo/10-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: f4df3d0bb3f361ef3ff22052003fbcbaadb7f1a22f2777f87c30ad9355622192; role: concept -->

No finite iteration marks a magical point of exact stationarity, and discarding states cannot repair a transition that misses part of the target.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Omitting the first 1,000 states here follows the declared reference computation. In adaptive samplers, *warmup* also tunes the transition rule. No finite iteration marks a magical point of exact stationarity, and discarding states cannot repair a transition that misses part of the target.

## Metropolis--Hastings sampling

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings.qmd; note-sha256: fcb4ce6af063fbf3fdc31b0a553d113cae2de18ef0a38497dd1b0b020d1c3ce1; role: concept -->

## Proposal and acceptance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings.qmd; note-sha256: fcb4ce6af063fbf3fdc31b0a553d113cae2de18ef0a38497dd1b0b020d1c3ce1; role: math -->

At current state $\eta^{(s)}$, draw a proposal

$$
\eta'\sim q(\eta'\mid\eta^{(s)}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

At current state $\eta^{(s)}$, draw a proposal

$$
\eta'\sim q(\eta'\mid\eta^{(s)}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings.qmd
:::

## Proposal and acceptance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings.qmd; note-sha256: fcb4ce6af063fbf3fdc31b0a553d113cae2de18ef0a38497dd1b0b020d1c3ce1; role: math -->

For posterior density kernel $\widetilde f$, form

$$
r
=
\frac{
\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)
q(\eta^{(s)}\mid\eta')
}{
\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)}\mid\mathbf y)
q(\eta'\mid\eta^{(s)})
}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For posterior density kernel $\widetilde f$, form

$$
r
=
\frac{
\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)
q(\eta^{(s)}\mid\eta')
}{
\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)}\mid\mathbf y)
q(\eta'\mid\eta^{(s)})
}.
$$

## Proposal and acceptance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings.qmd; note-sha256: fcb4ce6af063fbf3fdc31b0a553d113cae2de18ef0a38497dd1b0b020d1c3ce1; role: math -->

The unknown posterior normalizer also cancels, so the log acceptance ratio is

$$
\log r
=
\log\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)
-
\log\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)}\mid\mathbf y).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Accept when $U<\min(1,r)$ for $U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$; otherwise retain $\eta^{(s)}$. For the symmetric normal random walk, the two $q$ terms cancel. The unknown posterior normalizer also cancels, so the log acceptance ratio is

$$
\log r
=
\log\widetilde f(\eta'\mid\mathbf y)
-
\log\widetilde f(\eta^{(s)}\mid\mathbf y).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/metropolis-hastings.qmd
:::

## Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: concept -->

**Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)** instead uses the gradient of the passage-level Student-t model log posterior to build a coordinated proposal in $(\mu,\log\sigma)$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Random-walk MH proposes without consulting the target's local geometry. **Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)** instead uses the gradient of the passage-level Student-t model log posterior to build a coordinated proposal in $(\mu,\log\sigma)$.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd

## Potential, kinetic, and total energy {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: math -->

Let $q$ denote unconstrained parameters and let $\rho$ be an auxiliary momentum. The potential energy is

$$
U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $q$ denote unconstrained parameters and let $\rho$ be an auxiliary momentum. The potential energy is

$$
U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y).
$$

## Potential, kinetic, and total energy {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: math -->

For unit mass, draw $\rho\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and define

$$
K(\rho)=\frac12\rho^\mathsf T\rho,
\qquad
H(q,\rho)=U(q)+K(\rho).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For unit mass, draw $\rho\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and define

$$

H(q,\rho)=U(q)+K(\rho).

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/05-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: concept -->

It supplies a direction in which to construct a proposal.

## Potential, kinetic, and total energy {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: math -->

Hamilton's equations are

$$
\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=\rho,
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm d\rho}{\mathrm dt}=-\nabla U(q).
$$

## Leapfrog integration {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/08-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: math -->

For step size $\epsilon$, one leapfrog step is

$$
\rho_{t+\frac12}
=
\rho_t-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_t),
$$

$$
q_{t+1}=q_t+\epsilon\rho_{t+\frac12},
$$

$$
\rho_{t+1}
=
\rho_{t+\frac12}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_{t+1}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For step size $\epsilon$, one leapfrog step is

$$
\rho_{t+\frac12}
=
\rho_t-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_t),
$$

$$
q_{t+1}=q_t+\epsilon\rho_{t+\frac12},
$$

$$
\rho_{t+1}
=
\rho_{t+\frac12}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_{t+1}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd
:::

## Leapfrog integration {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo/09-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd; note-sha256: 9c923c357fe4fd46c9124010ffd20ac912458f14b387c3e18a8e6758272d2132; role: math -->

The half steps make the integrator reversible and volume preserving. Numerical integration changes the Hamiltonian slightly, so HMC accepts the endpoint with

$$
\alpha
=
\min\left\{1,
\exp[H(q,\rho)-H(q^*,\rho^*)]
\right\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The half steps make the integrator reversible and volume preserving. Numerical integration changes the Hamiltonian slightly, so HMC accepts the endpoint with

$$
\alpha
=
\min\left\{1,
\exp[H(q,\rho)-H(q^*,\rho^*)]
\right\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd
:::

## General kinetic energy {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/mass-matrix-geometry/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/mass-matrix-geometry.qmd; note-sha256: 57d3dada55ab81e418cddee89cde8044548f879a8f46415996f38f764c77f049; role: math -->

The position equation becomes

$$
\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=M^{-1}\rho,
$$

and the leapfrog position update is

$$
q_{t+1}=q_t+\epsilon M^{-1}\rho_{t+\frac12}.
$$

Because the velocity is $v=M^{-1}\rho$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(v)
=M^{-1}MM^{-1}=M^{-1}.
$$

::: {.notes}

A unit matrix treats all directions as equally scaled and uncorrelated. A diagonal matrix supplies separate scales but no rotation. A dense matrix can also represent global linear correlation. One constant dense matrix cannot remove curvature that changes across the posterior.

The matrix improves computation; it does not alter the 55 passage summaries or repair the passage-level Student-t model's aggregation limits.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Stan estimates a regularized inverse mass matrix during warmup, then holds it fixed during retained sampling. Adaptation must stop because changing the transition indefinitely could change its stationary distribution. ## The No-U-Turn Sampler

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/no-u-turn-sampler/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/no-u-turn-sampler.qmd; note-sha256: 77cf65cfe4099f09cbc5bc5e8cd1a4f02a0091d76f5e27434b6f8202890470f3; role: concept -->

Hoffman and Gelman (2014) introduced the original algorithm; Stan uses a multinomial variant described in its reference manual.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A static HMC transition requires a fixed number of leapfrog steps. The **No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)** chooses trajectory length during each transition. Hoffman and Gelman (2014) introduced the original algorithm; Stan uses a multinomial variant described in its reference manual.

[Sources]

https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/hoffman14a.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html
:::

## Growing and stopping a trajectory

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/no-u-turn-sampler/03-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/no-u-turn-sampler.qmd; note-sha256: 77cf65cfe4099f09cbc5bc5e8cd1a4f02a0091d76f5e27434b6f8202890470f3; role: concept -->

The tree constructs one transition; its internal states are not additional posterior draws.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

NUTS extends an HMC path forward or backward and organizes candidate states in a balanced binary tree. Increasing tree depth by one doubles the intended path length, though a turning condition or divergence may stop it early. The tree constructs one transition; its internal states are not additional posterior draws.

[Sources]

https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/hoffman14a.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html
:::

Let $q^-$ and $q^+$ be the trajectory endpoints and define

$$
\Delta q=q^+-q^-.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $q^-$ and $q^+$ be the trajectory endpoints and define

$$
\Delta q=q^+-q^-.
$$

An endpoint turning check examines

$$
\Delta q^\mathsf TM^{-1}\rho^-
\qquad\text{and}\qquad

When one becomes negative, momentum at that endpoint points back across the path.

## Implementing the passage-level Student-t model in Stan

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/stan/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/stan.qmd; note-sha256: ed31f368e2c69ba8dd754599960634c0662e8bbfb67f2ac3c676c7334943f64e; role: concept -->

The passage-level Student-t program below corresponds exactly to the robust model introduced on the nonconjugate-posterior page.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Stan samples a posterior after the analyst declares data, parameters, and density contributions. The passage-level Student-t program below corresponds exactly to the robust model introduced on the nonconjugate-posterior page.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/
:::

## The complete program

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/stan/03-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/stan.qmd; note-sha256: ed31f368e2c69ba8dd754599960634c0662e8bbfb67f2ac3c676c7334943f64e; role: concept -->

In the model block, each tilde statement adds a log-density contribution to Stan's `target`; it does not simulate a value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The data block contains the 55 observed passage contrasts and the empirically calibrated prior scales. The parameters block declares the unknown location and positive scale. In the model block, each tilde statement adds a log-density contribution to Stan's `target`; it does not simulate a value.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/
:::

## The complete program

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/stan/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/stan.qmd; note-sha256: ed31f368e2c69ba8dd754599960634c0662e8bbfb67f2ac3c676c7334943f64e; role: concept -->

Stan transforms this constrained parameter internally and applies the required Jacobian on its unconstrained sampling scale.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The half-normal prior is represented by the lower bound on `sigma` together with a zero-centered normal density. Stan transforms this constrained parameter internally and applies the required Jacobian on its unconstrained sampling scale.

[Sources]

https://mc-stan.org/

## Cross-chain agreement

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: concept -->

The **$\widehat R$ statistic** compares between-chain variation with within-chain variation: values near one are consistent with chain agreement, while larger values indicate persistent disagreement.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The trace and rank plots compare chains for the passage-level Student-t model visually. The **$\widehat R$ statistic** compares between-chain variation with within-chain variation: values near one are consistent with chain agreement, while larger values indicate persistent disagreement.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

## The basic variance ratio {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: math -->

For $M$ chains with $N$ draws each, let $\overline\mu_m$ and $s_m^2$ be the mean and variance in chain $m$. The average within-chain variance is

$$
W=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^Ms_m^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $M$ chains with $N$ draws each, let $\overline\mu_m$ and $s_m^2$ be the mean and variance in chain $m$. The average within-chain variance is

$$
W=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^Ms_m^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

## The basic variance ratio {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: math -->

The scaled between-chain variance is

$$
B=N\operatorname{Var}[\overline\mu_1,\ldots,\overline\mu_M].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The scaled between-chain variance is

$$
B=N\operatorname{Var}[\overline\mu_1,\ldots,\overline\mu_M].
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

## The basic variance ratio {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: math -->

Combining them gives

$$
\widehat V=\frac{N-1}{N}W+\frac1NB,
\qquad
\widehat R=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V}{W}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Combining them gives

$$
\widehat V=\frac{N-1}{N}W+\frac1NB,
\qquad
\widehat R=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V}{W}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

## Calculating $\widehat R$ for the passage-level Student-t model

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/06-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: concept -->

The modern rank-normalized split values for both parameters of the passage-level Student-t model are at most 1.0001.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The textbook calculation gives $\widehat R=$ 0.999615 for $\mu$. The modern rank-normalized split values for both parameters of the passage-level Student-t model are at most 1.0001.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

## Modern refinements

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/07-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: concept -->

Current software reports the larger rank-normalized split and folded values, following Vehtari et al. (2021).

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Splitting each chain into early and late halves makes within-chain drift visible as disagreement among sequences. Rank normalization improves behavior for skewed or heavy-tailed draws. Folding replaces each value with its absolute distance from the pooled median, making the diagnostic sensitive to chains with similar centers but different spreads. Current software reports the larger rank-normalized split and folded values, following Vehtari et al. (2021).

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

## Modern refinements

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/08-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: concept -->

It is also quantity specific: derived quantities and scale parameters require their own checks.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A value below 1.01 is an operational threshold, not a convergence theorem. Chains can agree in the same incomplete region, and $\widehat R$ does not measure posterior magnitude or model adequacy. It is also quantity specific: derived quantities and scale parameters require their own checks.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/09-question; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: question -->

## Cross-chain agreement: answer 1

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/rhat/10-answer; notes-page: statistical-inference/rhat.qmd; note-sha256: e11ad3077c97edf1315c3d6391f4b20141e3f09253baefa9c0d71652d9047a70; role: answer -->

Because $B=N\operatorname{Var}[\overline\mu_1,\ldots,\overline\mu_M]$, large dispersion among chain means makes $B$ large, with that dispersion scaled by the common chain length $N$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Because $B=N\operatorname{Var}[\overline\mu_1,\ldots,\overline\mu_M]$, large dispersion among chain means makes $B$ large, with that dispersion scaled by the common chain length $N$.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1214/20-BA1221

## Autocorrelation in a Markov chain

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/autocorrelation/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd; note-sha256: 5de933afef6a7df9620de6562e1cd46fae1a0b7969d3be9aa319abdd35d1fb62; role: concept -->

**Autocorrelation** measures the association between a saved sequence and a shifted copy of itself.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The chains for the passage-level Student-t model agree across initializations, but adjacent draws remain dependent. **Autocorrelation** measures the association between a saved sequence and a shifted copy of itself.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd
:::

## Autocorrelation in a Markov chain {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/autocorrelation/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd; note-sha256: 5de933afef6a7df9620de6562e1cd46fae1a0b7969d3be9aa319abdd35d1fb62; role: math -->

For a stationary scalar sequence, the autocorrelation at lag $t$ is

$$
\rho_t
=
\operatorname{Corr}(\Theta_s,\Theta_{s+t}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a stationary scalar sequence, the autocorrelation at lag $t$ is

$$
\rho_t
=
\operatorname{Corr}(\Theta_s,\Theta_{s+t}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/autocorrelation/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd; note-sha256: 5de933afef6a7df9620de6562e1cd46fae1a0b7969d3be9aa319abdd35d1fb62; role: concept -->

A chain of 1,000 draws supplies 999 lag-one pairs and 990 lag-ten pairs.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Lag one compares adjacent draws; lag ten compares draws ten transitions apart. A chain of 1,000 draws supplies 999 lag-one pairs and 990 lag-ten pairs.

## The production passage-level Student-t model autocorrelation functions

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/autocorrelation/06-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd; note-sha256: 5de933afef6a7df9620de6562e1cd46fae1a0b7969d3be9aa319abdd35d1fb62; role: concept -->

High autocorrelation need not imply the wrong stationary distribution, but it reduces finite-run precision.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Rapid decay suggests that dependence weakens over a small number of transitions. Slow decay means that information about one state persists across later states. High autocorrelation need not imply the wrong stationary distribution, but it reduces finite-run precision.

## The production passage-level Student-t model autocorrelation functions

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/autocorrelation/07-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/autocorrelation.qmd; note-sha256: 5de933afef6a7df9620de6562e1cd46fae1a0b7969d3be9aa319abdd35d1fb62; role: concept -->

Thinning may make the retained sequence look less correlated, but it discards information and creates none.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Negative autocorrelation can make alternating values offset one another and improve precision for some averages. Thus the complete sequence matters, not only lag one. Thinning may make the retained sequence look less correlated, but it discards information and creates none.

## Effective sample size

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

**Effective sample size** (ESS) approximates the independent-draw count that would give comparable Monte Carlo precision for a particular quantity.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Dependent draws contain less information about many posterior summaries than the same number of independent target draws. **Effective sample size** (ESS) approximates the independent-draw count that would give comparable Monte Carlo precision for a particular quantity.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## From autocorrelation to ESS {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/03-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: math -->

For a stationary scalar sequence of $S$ draws,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}
\approx
\frac{S}{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a stationary scalar sequence of $S$ draws,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}
\approx
\frac{S}{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## From autocorrelation to ESS

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/04-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

Positive dependence increases it and reduces ESS; negative dependence can make ESS exceed the raw draw count for some summaries.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The denominator is the integrated autocorrelation time. Positive dependence increases it and reduces ESS; negative dependence can make ESS exceed the raw draw count for some summaries.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## From autocorrelation to ESS {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/05-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: math -->

For a function $g(\Theta)$ with posterior standard deviation $\sigma_g$,

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}
\approx
\frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ESS}}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a function $g(\Theta)$ with posterior standard deviation $\sigma_g$,

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}
\approx
\frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ESS}}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## From autocorrelation to ESS

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/06-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

This is uncertainty in a numerical estimate of a posterior mean, not posterior uncertainty about a linguistic quantity.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This is uncertainty in a numerical estimate of a posterior mean, not posterior uncertainty about a linguistic quantity.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/07-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

The calculation computes a textbook positive-sequence estimate for chain one's $\mu$ draws, then obtains modern four-chain bulk and tail ESS from `posterior`.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

the calculation computes a textbook positive-sequence estimate for chain one's $\mu$ draws, then obtains modern four-chain bulk and tail ESS from `posterior`.

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/08-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

These are different estimators applied to different collections of draws, so their difference is not a disagreement.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The one-chain textbook value is 665. The modern bulk ESS for $\mu$ is 2867, while its tail ESS is 2355. These are different estimators applied to different collections of draws, so their difference is not a disagreement.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/09-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

This separation is the point of ESS.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The posterior standard deviation of $\mu$ is 0.007075, whereas the estimated MCSE of its posterior mean is 0.000132. This separation is the point of ESS.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/10-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

A chain can move adequately through the center but rarely reach a tail, so the appropriate diagnostic depends on the reported summary.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Bulk ESS uses rank-normalized draws and is useful for location summaries. Tail ESS targets information relevant to the 5% and 95% quantiles. A chain can move adequately through the center but rarely reach a tail, so the appropriate diagnostic depends on the reported summary.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd
:::

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size/11-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/effective-sample-size.qmd; note-sha256: 767060b3c88e3e843066ebc698e614a7552bd1cf64e53e6ba03755b378e8cb36; role: concept -->

It cannot add evidence to the passage-level Student-t model or narrow its posterior target.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

ESS counts simulation information, not passages, word positions, or readers. Running longer can increase ESS and reduce MCSE. It cannot add evidence to the passage-level Student-t model or narrow its posterior target.

## Divergent Hamiltonian transitions

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd; note-sha256: 86b1091f34dc4cc93eb21a4ee1fecc94c361e42bd3f2200f42fc214b91fdb8f7; role: concept -->

We demonstrate the warning with a deliberately coarse computation on the same passage-level Student-t model used throughout this sequence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **divergent transition** occurs when numerical integration error exceeds Stan's threshold. It indicates that a trajectory may not have followed the target geometry reliably in one region. We demonstrate the warning with a deliberately coarse computation on the same passage-level Student-t model used throughout this sequence.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd
:::

## Energy error and geometry {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions/04-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd; note-sha256: 86b1091f34dc4cc93eb21a4ee1fecc94c361e42bd3f2200f42fc214b91fdb8f7; role: math -->

Rapidly changing curvature can make one step size inaccurate in a narrow region even if it works elsewhere. In a hierarchical model, for instance,

$$
u_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2)
$$

can produce a narrow region when $\tau$ is near zero and a wider region when $\tau$ is large.

::: {.notes}

## Production and stress computations

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions/07-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd; note-sha256: 86b1091f34dc4cc93eb21a4ee1fecc94c361e42bd3f2200f42fc214b91fdb8f7; role: concept -->

This run demonstrates a numerical warning; it is not a second inferential fit and is not evidence of a defect in the production model.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The production passage-level Student-t fit uses adapted NUTS. A deliberately coarse run uses the same complete passage set, likelihood, priors, and data-derived initial region, but disables warmup and adaptation, uses a unit metric, fixes step size at 0.03, and caps tree depth at 7. This run demonstrates a numerical warning; it is not a second inferential fit and is not evidence of a defect in the production model.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd
:::

## Responding to a real divergence

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions/10-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd; note-sha256: 86b1091f34dc4cc93eb21a4ee1fecc94c361e42bd3f2200f42fc214b91fdb8f7; role: concept -->

Refit and recheck all diagnostics.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

First locate the marked draws in theoretically relevant parameter pairs. Then inspect parameter identification, predictor scales, and parameterization. Increasing `adapt_delta` usually reduces step size and may repair modest integration error; reparameterization may be needed when curvature changes substantially. Refit and recheck all diagnostics.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/divergent-transitions.qmd
:::

## Three passage-level Student-t model outputs {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/generated-quantities/06-math; notes-page: statistical-inference/generated-quantities.qmd; note-sha256: 612d1fa250d18d39d56794ecc8ea118d48f9990de06ec54a32fdd480f8556012; role: math -->

For passage $j$, the replication and log-likelihood contribution are

$$
Y_j^{\mathrm{rep},(s)}
\sim t_4(\mu^{(s)},\sigma^{(s)}),
$$

$$
\ell_j^{(s)}
=
\log t_4(y_j\mid\mu^{(s)},\sigma^{(s)}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## Posterior predictive checks

<!-- generated-slide-id: statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks/02-concept; notes-page: statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks.qmd; note-sha256: a1ee5eaebd6b1ec0783f13eef8fb234309a0871c2f05b9d3e611b5d34e5ba633; role: concept -->

It criticizes one implication of the passage-level Student-t model rather than assigning a global fit label.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **posterior predictive check** compares an observed feature with the same feature in data generated from the fitted model. It criticizes one implication of the passage-level Student-t model rather than assigning a global fit label.

[Sources]

Course note: statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks.qmd

$$
(\mu^{(s)},\sigma^{(s)})
\sim f(\mu,\sigma\mid\mathbf y),

then

\sim t_4(\mu^{(s)},\sigma^{(s)}),
\qquad j=1,\ldots,55.
